questions.question: What is the difference between == for primitives vs == for objects in Java?
questions.title: == for Primitives vs Objects in Java
questions.direct_answer: For **primitives**, `==` compares the actual **values** directly. For **objects**, `==` compares **references** (memory addresses) — it checks whether both variables point to the same object, not whether the objects have equal content. This split is one of the most common sources of bugs in Java.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java's value vs reference semantics — the foundational distinction that affects every data structure decision
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using == to compare String or Integer values and being confused when identical-looking values return false
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Integer cache (-128 to 127) as a gotcha where == sometimes works for objects, making the bug even harder to spot

sections.title: Start Here: What == Actually Checks Depends on Where the Value Lives
sections.content:
The `==` operator checks whether two things are the **same**. That is its whole job.

But Java stores two kinds of data, and the word "same" means something different for each — which is why `==` confuses almost every beginner.

First, why `==` exists at all. In code you **constantly need to ask** "are these two things equal?" — is this the right number, is this the same user. `==` is the operator that asks that question.

Here is how it works for simple values. When you write `int a = 5;`, Java keeps the number in a small slot of memory called the **stack**, and the value `5` sits directly inside that slot. So when you ask `a == b`, Java looks inside both slots and compares the raw numbers. Two slots holding `5` are equal, and that is never surprising.

Objects are different. When you write `String s = new String("hello");`, the actual text lives in a larger memory area called the **heap**, and the stack slot only holds an **address** — a number that points to where the object sits. Think of it like a house: the heap is the house, and the variable just holds a slip of paper with the street address on it. When you compare two objects with `==`, Java compares the two slips of paper, not the houses. So two separate `"hello"` objects have different addresses, and `==` returns `false` even though the text is identical.

Now the interview nuance. Java quietly reuses some objects to save memory. Identical text **literals** like `"hello"` share one pooled object, and small `Integer` values from `-128` to `127` are cached and reused. When that happens, both variables point to the same address, so `==` accidentally returns `true`.

And that is the gotcha: `==` on objects **works sometimes and fails other times**, with the exact same code. It passes your tests with small numbers or pooled strings, then breaks in production when the value comes from user input or climbs past `127`.

> **The safe habit is simple** — use `==` only for primitives and `null` checks, and use `.equals()` whenever you care about an object's content.

sections.title: Stack vs Heap: What == Actually Sees
sections.content:
This diagram shows what the JVM memory looks like when you compare two ints versus two Strings. For the ints, each stack slot contains the value directly — `==` sees `5 == 5` and returns `true`. For the Strings created with `new`, each stack slot contains an arrow to a different heap object — `==` sees two different addresses and returns `false`, even though the text is identical. For String literals, both stack slots point to the same interned pool object, so `==` returns `true` — the sneaky case. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph STACK["Stack (local variables)"] A["int a = 5
slot holds: 5"] B["int b = 5
slot holds: 5"] S1["String s1
slot holds: addr-0xA1"] S2["String s2
slot holds: addr-0xB2"] L1["String lit1
slot holds: addr-0xC3"] L2["String lit2
slot holds: addr-0xC3"] end subgraph HEAP["Heap (objects)"] ObjA["String object
'hello' at 0xA1"] ObjB["String object
'hello' at 0xB2"] Pool["String pool
'hello' at 0xC3
(shared)"] end A -- "== compares 5 vs 5 → true" --> B S1 -- "addr-0xA1" --> ObjA S2 -- "addr-0xB2" --> ObjB S1 -- "== compares 0xA1 vs 0xB2 → false" --> S2 L1 -- "addr-0xC3" --> Pool L2 -- "addr-0xC3" --> Pool L1 -- "== compares 0xC3 vs 0xC3 → true" --> L2 ``` The key takeaway: `==` never looks inside the heap object. It only compares what is in the stack slot. For objects that means comparing addresses, which is almost never what you want for equality.

sections.content:
amber|== on primitives|~Compares values|5 == 5 is true|works for int/double/char|no method needed
blue|== on objects|~Compares references|same object in memory|content is ignored|two equal-looking objects are false
emerald|.equals()|~Compares content|the safe choice|override in custom classes|use for String/Integer

sections.title: Primitives vs Objects with ==
sections.content:
| Aspect | Primitives (`int`, `double`, `boolean`) | Objects (`String`, `Integer`, custom) |
|---|---|---|
| What `==` compares | Actual values in memory | Memory addresses (references) |
| When `==` is `true` | Values are mathematically equal | Both variables point to same object |
| Typical use case | Numeric comparisons, boolean checks | Identity checks, null checks |
| For content equality | Use `==` directly | Must use `.equals()` |
| Example `true` case | `int a=5, b=5; a==b` | `String s2 = s1; s1==s2` |

sections.title: Wrong — == on Integer objects looks fine until it isn't
sections.content:
The most dangerous version of this bug is the one that *passes* in testing. Because `==` on objects compares addresses, and the JVM happens to reuse `Integer` objects for small values, the same line of code can return `true` or `false` depending only on the number it sees.

```java
Integer a = 127, b = 127;
System.out.println(a == b); // true  — both point to one cached object, deceptive

Integer x = 200, y = 200;
System.out.println(x == y); // false — separate heap objects beyond the cache
```

The comparison logic never changed — only the value did. That is why an `Integer == Integer` check can sail through unit tests built on small numbers and then fail the first time real data carries an ID above 127.

sections.title: Right — compare wrapper values with equals()
sections.content:
The fix sidesteps the address question entirely. `.equals()` on an `Integer` reads the wrapped `int` and compares the numbers, so it returns the right answer whether or not the cache was involved.

```java
Integer x = 200, y = 200;
System.out.println(x.equals(y));                     // true — compares the wrapped value
System.out.println(java.util.Objects.equals(x, y)); // true — same result, and null-safe
```

Reach for `.equals()` for content, and `Objects.equals(...)` when either side might be `null` — it null-checks first instead of throwing. The only job left for `==` on objects is asking "are these literally the same instance?"

sections.title: When to Use Each Comparison Approach
sections.content:
Use `==` for **primitives** — it's the only way to compare `int`, `double`, `boolean`, `char` values.

Use `==` for **objects only when checking identity or null**: `if (user == null)` or `if (currentUser == loggedInUser)` where you specifically need the exact same instance.

Use **`.equals()`** for object content comparison — checking:
- if two strings have the same characters
- if two `Integer` wrappers hold the same number
- or if two custom objects are logically equivalent

In a login system, use `userName.equals(inputName)`, never `userName == inputName`.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **String comparison with `==`**: `if (userName == "admin")` sometimes works (string interning) but breaks when the string comes from user input or a file — an intermittent bug.
- **Ignoring the Integer cache**: `Integer x = 100; Integer y = 100; x == y` is `true`, but at `200` it's `false`. `==` seems to work for `Integer` until values exceed 127.
- **Confusing equals() direction**: `userName.equals("admin")` throws `NullPointerException` if `userName` is null; use `"admin".equals(userName)` or `Objects.equals(...)`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Primitives** — `==` compares values directly; `5 == 5` is `true`, no method needed.
- **Objects** — `==` compares memory addresses; two separate `"hello"` objects return `false`.
- **Stack vs heap** — primitives store their value on the stack; objects store an address on the stack and data on the heap.
- **String interning** — literal strings share a pooled object, so `==` appears to work — until it doesn't.
- **Null safety** — `x == null` is safe; `x.equals(y)` crashes if `x` is null.
- **Best practice** — never use `==` for `String`, `Integer`, or custom objects unless you need reference equality.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
It really comes down to **where the value lives**. A primitive like `int` sits directly in its slot, so double equals just compares the **raw numbers** — two `int`s holding `5` are equal, no surprise there.

An object variable doesn't hold the object; it holds the **address** of where that object lives on the heap. So double equals on two objects compares addresses, not contents — two separate `String` objects both spelling `hello` sit at different addresses, so it's `false` even though the text matches.

What makes this nasty is that it **sometimes looks like it works**. Identical `String` literals get pooled into one object, and Java caches `Integer` values from minus `128` to `127` — so double equals is `true` for `100` but `false` for `200`, with the exact same code. That sails through tests on small numbers and then breaks in production. **My rule is simple**: double equals only for primitives and `null` checks, and `equals` for any object's content.

questions.question: What is the Integer cache in Java and how does it affect == comparisons?
questions.title: Integer Cache in Java — The -128 to 127 Gotcha
questions.direct_answer: Java **caches Integer objects for values -128 to 127**. When you autobox an int in this range, Java returns the same cached `Integer` object instead of creating a new one. So `==` returns `true` for two `Integer` variables with values in this range but `false` outside it — a classic interview trap.

sections.title: Start Here: Why Java Reuses Some Integer Objects and Not Others
sections.content:
The **Integer cache** is a small set of `Integer` objects that Java builds once and reuses, instead of creating a brand-new one every time you use a small number.

To see why it exists, you first need one word: **autoboxing**. Java has two ways to hold a whole number. A primitive `int` is a raw number. An `Integer` is a full **object** that wraps that number so it can be stored in places that only accept objects, like a list. When you write `Integer x = 42;`, Java automatically turns the raw `42` into an `Integer` object for you. That automatic conversion is called autoboxing, and behind the scenes it calls `Integer.valueOf(42)`.

Here is how the cache works. Creating an object costs memory, and tiny numbers like `0`, `1`, or `100` get used constantly — loop counters, flags, status codes. So when the program starts, Java pre-builds one `Integer` object for every value from **-128 to 127** and keeps them ready. Whenever `Integer.valueOf` is asked for a number in that range, it hands back the same shared object instead of making a new one. Ask for `100` a hundred times and you get the same object every time.

Why those exact numbers? `-128` to `127` is the range of a `byte` — the smallest, **most common integers** in real programs. Caching them removes thousands of pointless object creations in a typical run.

Now **the gotcha**, and it is a famous one. Remember that `==` on objects compares memory addresses, not values. If two `Integer` variables both hold `100`, they point to the same cached object, so `==` returns `true`. Do the same with `200` — which is outside the cache — and Java makes two separate objects at two different addresses, so `==` returns `false`, even though both hold `200`. Same code, opposite result, just because the number changed.

That is why this bug slips through tests built on small numbers and then surprises you in production, once a real ID or quantity crosses `127`. One last nuance: the upper bound is tunable through the `-XX:AutoBoxCacheMax` JVM flag, so never assume the cache ends at exactly `127`.

> **The fix is absolute**: never compare `Integer` objects with `==`. Use `.equals()`, which reads the wrapped value and is always correct.

sections.title: Inside the Integer Cache: What Happens at 100 vs 200
sections.content:
The diagram below shows the cache as a pre-loaded block of 256 `Integer` objects that live in the JVM's class-loading area. When autoboxing produces a value in range, both variables get a reference to the same slot — `==` sees identical addresses. Outside the range, every autobox call allocates a fresh heap object — `==` sees different addresses.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph JVM_STARTUP["JVM startup — Integer cache"]
        C1["Integer(-128)"]
        C2["Integer(-127)"]
        CDOT["... 254 more objects ..."]
        C127["Integer(127)"]
    end

    subgraph HEAP_NEW["Heap — new allocations (outside cache)"]
        N1["Integer(200) — object A"]
        N2["Integer(200) — object B"]
    end

    A100["Integer a = 100"] -- "valueOf(100) → cached slot" --> C1
    B100["Integer b = 100"] -- "valueOf(100) → same cached slot" --> C1
    A100 -- "a == b → same address → TRUE" --> B100

    X200["Integer x = 200"] -- "valueOf(200) → new object" --> N1
    Y200["Integer y = 200"] -- "valueOf(200) → new object" --> N2
    X200 -- "x == y → different addresses → FALSE" --> Y200
```

The safe rule that makes this diagram irrelevant: always call `.equals()`. It compares the held `int` value, not the address, so it is correct regardless of whether the cache was involved.

sections.title: Integer Cache at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Integer cache|~-128 to 127 reused|autobox returns cached|saves memory|common small ints
blue|In range|~== works|Integer 100 == 100 is true|same object|deceptive
emerald|Out of range|~== breaks|Integer 200 == 200 is false|new objects|bug in production
rose|Other types|~Also cached|Byte Short Long -128..127|Character 0..127|always use equals

sections.title: Integer Cache Behavior
Wrong — relying on == for Integer passes only by luck
sections.content:
The trap is that the broken code and the working code look identical — the only difference is the number. When the value lands inside the cache, both variables share one object and `==` is `true`. Step outside the cache and you get two objects, so `==` flips to `false`.

```java
Integer a = 100, b = 100;
System.out.println(a == b); // true  — both autoboxed to the same cached object
Integer x = 200, y = 200;
System.out.println(x == y); // false — 200 is past 127, so two new objects
```

This is why the bug is so slippery: a test written with `1`, `2`, or `5` proves nothing, because every one of those values is cached. The failure only surfaces once a real ID, count, or amount crosses 127.

sections.title: Right — equals() compares value regardless of cache
sections.content:
Switching to `.equals()` makes the cache irrelevant. It reads the wrapped `int` and compares the numbers, so `200` equals `200` every time, no matter how the objects were created.

```java
Integer x = 200, y = 200;
System.out.println(x.equals(y));                     // true — compares the wrapped value
System.out.println(java.util.Objects.equals(x, y)); // true — null-safe too
```

The `-128` to `127` floor and ceiling are guaranteed by the spec, but the upper bound is tunable through the `-XX:AutoBoxCacheMax` JVM flag — another reason to never let correctness depend on `==`.

sections.title: How to Safely Compare Integer Objects
sections.content:
Always use **`.equals()`** to compare `Integer` values — it works regardless of cache range.

Use **`Objects.equals(a, b)`** for null-safe comparison when either value might be null.

Use `==` only for **null checks**: `if (userId == null)`. You can rely on the cache to save memory with small integers, but never write logic that depends on `==` behavior — it's an optimization detail.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Testing only with small numbers**: `==` comparison passes with `1, 2, 5` thanks to the cache, then production fails with larger IDs.
- **Confusion at the boundary**: `Integer.valueOf(100) == Integer.valueOf(100)` is `true` but at `200` it's `false`; this looks like broken autoboxing.
- **Assuming the cache is fixed**: the upper bound is configurable via a JVM flag — defensive code never relies on `==`.
- **Mixing primitives and wrappers**: `Integer x = 200; int y = 200; x == y` unboxes and is `true`, while two `Integer` 200s are `false`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cache range** — Java pre-creates `Integer` objects for -128 to 127.
- **== split** — `true` for cached values, `false` outside — the silent production bug.
- **Rationale** — small integers are extremely common; caching saves heap allocations.
- **Other cached types** — `Byte`, `Short`, `Long` (-128 to 127), `Character` (0 to 127).
- **Safe comparison** — always use `.equals()` for `Integer`, never `==`.
- **valueOf vs new** — `Integer.valueOf(n)` uses the cache; `new Integer(n)` bypasses it (and is deprecated).

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The thing that trips people up is that double equals on two `Integer`s can be `true` for one value and `false` for another, with **identical code**. That's the **Integer cache**.

When you autobox an `int`, the compiler calls `Integer` dot valueOf, and for values from minus `128` to `127` the JVM hands back a **pre-built, shared object** instead of allocating a new one. So two `Integer`s holding `100` point to the same object and double equals is `true`; two holding `200` are separate objects, so double equals is `false` even though both wrap `200`.

That's a **real bug pattern**, not just trivia. Code passes its tests because the test data uses small numbers, then breaks the moment an ID or a quantity climbs past `127`. The range isn't arbitrary either — minus `128` to `127` is exactly the `byte` range, the small integers programs lean on constantly, so caching them avoids a flood of allocations.

And the ceiling is tunable with the `AutoBoxCacheMax` flag, so you can't hardcode an assumption around `127`. **The takeaway is absolute**: never compare `Integer` objects with double equals — use `equals`, or `Objects` dot equals when null is in play. It costs nothing and it's always correct.
